metadata.title: Number Patterns, Telescoping Sums, and Structural Tricks
metadata.description: Simplify telescoping sums and repeated products by identifying valid cancellations and endpoints.
metadata.teachingApproach: Inspect neighboring terms; rewrite to expose cancellation; keep only verified endpoints; check term count.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 4 “Simplification,” printed pages 95–179. Approved scope: Teach structural simplification patterns in the chapter that are not ordinary operation chains: telescoping sums such as 1/[n(n+1)]=1/n−1/(n+1), cancellation across a sequence, repeated-product patterns, and simple cyclic or counting structures when they appear in this chapter. Show how to rewrite terms so the cancellation becomes visible, identify the first and last uncancelled parts, and avoid assuming a pattern without checking the terms. A learner should transform a structured sum or product into a simpler equivalent and verify the number of terms and endpoints. Do not expand this into a full sequences, series, or number-theory unit.

content.text:
Long expressions are sometimes short ideas written out term by term. A repeated structure can make most terms cancel, so look for a relationship between adjacent terms before calculating each fraction or product.

This lesson focuses on telescoping sums and repeated difference-of-squares products. The safe method is to rewrite terms in an equivalent form, show the cancellations explicitly, and verify the first and last surviving terms.

The goal is not to memorize a cancellation result, but to prove that the terms really cancel. Rewrite each term using an identity and line up the positive and negative pieces; then only the uncancelled endpoints remain.

A key identity is 1/[n(n+1)]=1/n−1/(n+1). To verify it, combine the right side: 1/n−1/(n+1)=[(n+1)−n]/[n(n+1)]=1/[n(n+1)]. Because the identity is exact, it can be used for each term of a sum.

For 1/(2×3)+1/(3×4)+…+1/(9×10), rewrite the terms as (1/2−1/3)+(1/3−1/4)+…+(1/9−1/10). The −1/3 cancels +1/3, −1/4 cancels +1/4, and so on. Only 1/2 and −1/10 remain, giving 1/2−1/10=4/10=2/5.

The endpoint check is important: the last denominator product is 9×10, so the final negative reciprocal is −1/10, not −1/9.

The identity works because the numerator of the combined difference becomes (n+1)−n=1. This is why the product n(n+1) becomes the difference of adjacent reciprocals; the numerator must be 1 for this exact form.

hints: For n=3 through 8, the uncancelled terms are 1/3 and −1/9.
inlineData.explanation: Rewrite each term as 1/n−1/(n+1). For n=3 through 8, all intermediate reciprocals cancel, leaving 1/3−1/9=2/9. Correct option: C.

content.text:
Rewrite each denominator product using the neighboring-reciprocal identity. Cancel matching intermediate values and preserve the first and last endpoints.

Try a new example using the same reasoning with different values.

When you list the terms, check that each negative reciprocal has a matching positive reciprocal from the next term. If an endpoint differs, correct it before adding.

inlineData.explanation: The sum is 1/4−1/7=(7−4)/28=3/28. The first and last surviving terms verify the cancellation endpoints. Correct option: D.

content.text:
Repeated difference of squares can also make a product collapse. The identity (1−u)(1+u)=1−u² applies with u=x, then x², then x⁴. Thus (1−x)(1+x)=1−x²; multiplying by (1+x²) gives 1−x⁴; multiplying by (1+x⁴) gives 1−x⁸; and multiplying by (1+x⁸) gives 1−x¹⁶.

Each factor has to match the current expression. The new factor is paired with 1 minus the corresponding power. Do not skip a stage or assume the exponent merely doubles without checking the next factor.

Cancellation is valid for equal and opposite terms in a sum, or common factors in a product/fraction. It is not valid to cancel terms across addition without rewriting the expression correctly.

At each product stage, treat the current power as u in (1−u)(1+u)=1−u². Since u is squared, each stage doubles the exponent: x becomes x², then x⁴, x⁸ and x¹⁶.

hints: Pair the first two factors as a difference of squares.
Each product creates the next power: 1−x², then 1−x⁴, then 1−x⁸, then 1−x^16.
inlineData.explanation: Use (1−u)(1+u)=1−u² repeatedly: the product becomes 1−x², then 1−x⁴, 1−x⁸, and finally 1−x¹⁶. Correct option: A.

content.text:
Use (a−b)(a+b)=a²−b² repeatedly. Keep each intermediate expression because it becomes one half of the next pair.

Try a new example using the same reasoning with different values.

Only multiply factors that match the difference-of-squares identity. The order matters because each intermediate expression creates the next pair.

hints: Multiply by 1+y² as another difference of squares.
inlineData.explanation: (1−y)(1+y)=1−y², and (1−y²)(1+y²)=1−y⁴. The first and last surviving terms verify the cancellation endpoints. Correct option: B.

content.text:
Check a proposed telescoping pattern against every term: the positive reciprocal from one term must exactly match the negative reciprocal from the next. Write the expansion for at least the first two terms and the final term before cancelling, especially when the sequence uses ellipses.

Verify a small case directly: 1/(2×3)+1/(3×4)=(1/2−1/3)+(1/3−1/4)=1/4. Direct addition also gives 1/6+1/12=2/12+1/12=3/12=1/4. Both approaches agree.

If a term does not match the pattern, it will not cancel. Do not apply the shortcut just because denominators look consecutive; verify the exact numerator and denominator structure.

For a small case, compare the shortcut with direct addition. Agreement verifies both the identity and the endpoints; this is a good way to catch a mistaken last denominator before attempting a longer sum.

inlineData.explanation: The endpoints are 1/5 and −1/9; the middle reciprocals cancel. Thus 1/5−1/9=(9−5)/45=4/45. Correct option: D.

content.text:
Use the endpoints rather than adding every fraction. Verify the endpoint subtraction with a common denominator, and confirm which values cancel.

Try a new example using the same reasoning with different values.

Expand the first two terms and last two terms if you are unsure. Seeing the same reciprocal with opposite signs is the evidence for cancellation.

hints: Replace each term with a difference of adjacent reciprocals.
inlineData.explanation: The sum telescopes to 1/3−1/6=1/6. The first and last surviving terms verify the cancellation endpoints. Correct option: B.

content.text:
You have completed Number Patterns, Telescoping Sums, and Structural Tricks.

Verify the identity before using it, expand enough terms to see the cancellations, and keep the first and last uncancelled pieces. In repeated products, apply the identity to complete matching factors one stage at a time.

Always check endpoints and term count; these are the most common sources of mistakes in a telescoping calculation.

For consecutive terms from n=k through n=m, the telescoping sum is 1/k−1/(m+1). The last endpoint is one larger than the final value of n because each term is 1/n−1/(n+1).

For n=5 through 14, the result is 1/5−1/15=3/15−1/15=2/15. Count the first and last terms explicitly: there are ten terms, but the surviving endpoints are determined by the first n and the last n+1, not by simply counting the terms.

When using a telescoping product, show each intermediate transformation too. A result that appears to cancel is only valid if the identity is applied to the entire matching factors in the right order.

For n=k through n=m, there are m−k+1 terms but the endpoint is 1/(m+1). Do not confuse the number of terms with the final successor in the denominator.
Find the sum of 1/[n(n+1)] for n=4,5,…,11.

inlineData.prompt: Find the sum of 1/[n(n+1)] for n=4,5,…,11.
hints: Use the telescoping identity from the first n value to the last.
inlineData.explanation: From n=4 through 11, the endpoints are 1/4 and −1/12. Their difference is 1/4−1/12=3/12−1/12=1/6. Correct option: A.

content.text:
The last term at n=m ends in 1/(m+1). After cancellation the endpoints are 1/k and −1/(m+1); use a common denominator to subtract.

Now try a new value set using the same method.

Write the last denominator product, such as 11×12, explicitly. It makes the surviving negative reciprocal immediately visible.
Find the sum of 1/[n(n+1)] for n=7,8,9,10,11.

inlineData.prompt: Find the sum of 1/[n(n+1)] for n=7,8,9,10,11.
hints: The positive terms cancel the next negative reciprocals.
inlineData.explanation: The sum is 1/7−1/12=(12−7)/84=5/84. The first and last surviving terms verify the cancellation endpoints. Correct option: C.
